title: The 2026 El Niño Is on Track to Be the Strongest on Record
gist: Berkeley Earth's Zeke Hausfather, using 667 simulations across 14 climate models, projects the 2026 El Nino peaking at 3.6C above normal in the Nino 3.4 region — roughly 0.8C beyond the 2015-16 record, when the entire spread between the first and fifth strongest events of the past 150 years is only about 0.5C. The knock-on estimates are 2027 global temperatures up to 1.7C above preindustrial and cumulative economic losses near $10 trillion by 2032.

insights.claim: Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather projects that the El Nino developing in the Pacific is very likely to be the strongest since reliable records began, potentially by a very large margin.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: A once-in-150-years climate shock is the kind of exogenous driver that reprices agricultural commodities, insurance, and emerging-market inflation.

insights.claim: The model average puts peak heat in the Nino 3.4 region at 3.6 degrees Celsius (6.5 Fahrenheit) above normal, exceeding the 2015-2016 record by approximately 0.8 degrees Celsius.

insights.claim: The forecast sits outside all observed history: the spread between the strongest and fifth-strongest El Nino of the past 150 years is only about 0.5 degrees Celsius, far less than the margin now projected.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: Historical-analogue-based risk models will systematically understate this event's impacts.

insights.claim: The analysis rests on 667 simulations benchmarked against historical records of the most intense El Nino events since 1877, and separates El Nino intensity from fossil-fuel-driven background warming to make super El Ninos comparable.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: Detrending against background warming is what makes the record claim defensible rather than an artifact of a warming baseline.

insights.claim: This year's El Nino is intensifying faster than the 1997-1998 super event and unlike 2015 it had no running start, since 2026 began with La Nina conditions in the Pacific.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: A cold start reaching record heat implies unusual forcing — raises the odds that models are still underestimating the peak.

insights.claim: El Nino heat takes time to propagate through the climate system, so the full effect of this year's Pacific heat on global average temperature will show up in 2027 rather than 2026.
